# Use TypeScript for the app and server

> **Decision:** Use TypeScript everywhere. **Because** the team already writes it. **Accepted cost:** a build step and type errors to fix before shipping. **Revisit if** the team moves to another language.

## Context and Problem Statement
Which language should fieldnotes be written in?

## Decision Drivers
- The team writes TypeScript every day (your answer)
- Express starter (seen in package.json)

## Considered Options
1. TypeScript
2. JavaScript

## Decision Outcome
Chosen: TypeScript, because the team already writes it and errors show up before users see them.

### Consequences
- Good, because type errors show up before users see them.
- Bad, because there is a build step to keep working.

## More Information
- Confidence: high; every driver is seen in the repo or answered.

decisions.scope: Covers identity method (password, magic link, external login, etc) and what user data is collected. Leaves storage tech and session format to other decisions.

decisions.scope: Covers database or file storage choice and table/schema shape for users and projects. Leaves hosting provider and session mechanism to others.

decisions.title: Choose session and authentication state mechanism
decisions.scope: Covers how logged-in state is maintained (server cookie session vs token), expiry, and logout/revocation. Leaves auth method itself to other decision.

decisions.title: Define project ownership and access rules

decisions.default: private projects owned by single user, no sharing in v1
decisions.why: Adding sharing/collaboration after launch requires a new permission system that is hard to retrofit without breaking existing data.

options.name: Email + password
options.summary: Users sign up with email and choose a password you store hashed

good.text: Familiar flow, works without external services

bad.text: You must hash passwords correctly and handle reset flow
You own breach risk and support for forgotten passwords

learn.what: You collect email and a password hash. On login you compare the hash using a slow hashing function. Sessions are then created separately.
learn.living_with: You manage password rules, reset emails, and secure storage. Users can log in even if email is down, after initial signup.

terms.meaning: One-way scrambled version of password that can't be reversed
Random data added before hashing to make each hash unique

options.name: Magic link via email
options.summary: No passwords; users get a one-time login link sent to their email

good.text: No password storage or hashing code needed
Collects only email, minimal personal data

bad.text: Login depends on email delivery and link expiry handling
Harder to support API clients or long-lived offline login

learn.what: User enters email, you create a short-lived token and email a link containing it. Clicking the link proves ownership and creates a session.
learn.living_with: Each login needs inbox access. You need an email sending service and to handle expired or reused links.

terms.meaning: Single-use URL that logs you in when clicked

learn.what: You redirect to a provider like Google. After approval, provider returns an ID and email you use to find or create local user.
learn.living_with: You configure client IDs, handle callback routes, and deal with provider outages. No local passwords to reset.

terms.meaning: Standard for letting users sign in via another service

options.name: SQLite file with two tables
options.summary: One local file holding users and projects tables with foreign keys.

good.text: No server to run, works with just Express and a driver
Easy to back up by copying file and to migrate to Postgres later

bad.text: Need to add better-sqlite3 or sqlite3 dependency and write migrations
Writes are single-writer, not ideal for heavy concurrent public use

learn.what: SQLite is a relational database stored in a single file. You create tables for users (id, email, password_hash) and projects (id, user_id, data) and use SQL queries.
learn.living_with: You check in migration scripts, not the DB file. Day to day you query with SQL and the file lives in your project data folder.

terms.meaning: A script that creates or changes tables safely
A column that links a project to its owner user

options.name: JSON files on disk
options.summary: Save users.json and projects.json, read/write with fs.

good.text: Zero dependencies, you already have file system
Easy to inspect files directly for debugging

bad.text: No atomic writes or queries, risk of corrupt file on crash
Hard to enforce ownership, search, or scale beyond one user

learn.what: You store all users in one JSON file and all projects in another. Node reads the file into memory, edits it, writes it back.
learn.living_with: You manage locking yourself and watch for file bloat. Backups are file copies and edits have no history.

terms.meaning: An operation that fully succeeds or fails, no half-written state

options.name: Managed Postgres database
options.summary: External Postgres service holding users and projects tables.

good.text: Proper relations, concurrent writes, ready for online hosting
Scales to public sign-up and sharing without rewriting storage

bad.text: Requires connection string, hosted service setup, and network access
You pay for hosting and manage backups and credentials outside code

learn.what: Postgres is a separate database server. Your app connects over a URL and stores users and projects in tables with SQL.
learn.living_with: You need env vars for connection, run migrations on deploy, and monitor the external service uptime.

terms.meaning: URL containing host, user, password for the database
Database run by a provider, not by your app code

options.name: One owner, private only
options.summary: Each saved project belongs to one user, only that user can view or edit.

good.text: Simple schema: projects table has owner_id only
Least risk of leaking data to other users

bad.text: No way to show a project to someone else
Adding sharing later requires new tables and UI

learn.what: A saved project is a record with owner_id, title, content, timestamps. Ownership is checked on every read and write: if logged-in user id != owner_id, deny.
learn.living_with: You log in and only see your projects. There is no share button. Support is just checking logs for owner mismatch.

terms.meaning: User id stored on project to say who owns it
Code that blocks request if user is not allowed

options.name: One owner, plus view-only share link
options.summary: One owner controls edit, but can create a random link that lets others view read-only.

good.text: Enables sharing without accounts for viewers
Easy upgrade path to full collaborators later

bad.text: Need to generate and store share tokens and handle revocation
Link can leak if forwarded, need to explain security

learn.what: Project still has one owner_id. Extra field share_token holds a random unguessable string. GET /p/:token shows read-only view without login.
learn.living_with: Owner sees a Share button to copy link and revoke it. Viewers cannot edit. You manage expired or leaked links.

terms.meaning: Long random code in URL that grants read-only access
Can view content but cannot change or delete

options.name: Owner plus explicit collaborators
options.summary: One owner plus a list of other users with viewer or editor roles per project.

good.text: Supports team workflows from day one
Granular roles make future paid or team features easier

bad.text: Requires join table for memberships and role checks on every request
More complex invite, removal, and leaving logic to maintain

learn.what: You have projects, users, and project_members table with project_id, user_id, role. Owner role can add/remove members. Checks allow view if member, edit if editor or owner.
learn.living_with: Project settings show member list and invite by email. Every edit path checks role. You handle invite errors and removed users.

terms.meaning: Another user added to a project with permission
Label like viewer or editor that decides what someone can do
